name: Chapter 11: Photosynthesis in Higher Plants
description: Early experiments, pigments, light reaction, Z scheme, chemiosmosis, Calvin cycle, C4 pathway, photorespiration, limiting factors

cards.term: What is photosynthesis?
cards.definition: A physico-chemical process by which green plants use light energy to drive the synthesis of organic compounds

cards.term: Why are green plants called autotrophs?
cards.definition: They synthesise their own food by photosynthesis

cards.term: Two reasons photosynthesis is important?
cards.definition: It is the primary source of all food on earth, and it releases oxygen into the atmosphere

cards.term: What three things did school experiments show are needed for photosynthesis?
cards.definition: Chlorophyll, light and CO₂

cards.term: Variegated leaf / half-covered leaf starch test shows what?
cards.definition: Photosynthesis occurs only in green parts and only in light

cards.term: Half-leaf experiment: what does KOH in the test tube do?
cards.definition: KOH absorbs CO₂; the enclosed part tests negative for starch, so CO₂ is required

cards.term: What did Priestley conclude from the bell-jar experiments (1770)?
cards.definition: Plants restore to the air whatever breathing animals and burning candles remove

cards.term: Describe Priestley's bell-jar observations (Figure 11.1).
cards.definition: A candle goes out and a mouse suffocates in a closed jar; with a mint plant inside, the candle burns and the mouse lives

cards.term: Which gas did Priestley discover, and when?
cards.definition: Oxygen, in 1774

cards.term: What did Jan Ingenhousz show?
cards.definition: Sunlight is essential; only the green parts of plants release oxygen

cards.term: How did Ingenhousz show that green parts release O₂?
cards.definition:
An aquatic plant in bright sunlight formed bubbles around green parts, not in the dark.
The bubbles were oxygen

cards.term: What did Julius von Sachs show (1854)?
cards.definition: Plants produce glucose (stored as starch); chlorophyll is in special bodies (later called chloroplasts)

cards.term: What did Engelmann's experiment show?
cards.definition: Aerobic bacteria gathered in blue and red light around Cladophora: the first action spectrum of photosynthesis

cards.term: Why did Engelmann use aerobic bacteria?
cards.definition: To detect the sites of O₂ evolution

cards.term: What did Cornelius van Niel show?
cards.definition:
Photosynthesis is a light-dependent reaction in which hydrogen from an oxidisable compound reduces CO₂.
The O₂ released by green plants comes from water, not CO₂

cards.term: van Niel's general equation?
cards.definition: 2H₂A + CO₂ → 2A + CH₂O + H₂O (with light)

cards.term: What is the hydrogen donor in purple and green sulphur bacteria? What is released?
cards.definition: H₂S; they release sulphur or sulphate, not O₂

cards.term: Balanced overall equation of photosynthesis?
cards.definition: 6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6H₂O + 6O₂ (with light)

cards.term: Why 12 H₂O in the photosynthesis equation?
cards.definition: All O₂ comes from water: 6 O₂ need 12 O atoms, so 12 H₂O are split; 6 H₂O are formed again

cards.term: How was it proved that O₂ comes from water?
cards.definition: Radioisotope techniques (labelled ¹⁸O in water appears in the released O₂)

cards.term: Is photosynthesis a single reaction?
cards.definition: No. The equation summarises a multistep process.

cards.term: Early photosynthesis experiments
cards.definition: Plants restore air (mint, mouse, candle): Priestley; Sunlight needed; green parts release O₂: Ingenhousz; Glucose made; chlorophyll in chloroplasts: Sachs; First action spectrum (Cladophora): Engelmann; O₂ comes from H₂O: van Niel

cards.term: Where does photosynthesis occur in a plant?
cards.definition: In green leaves, and also in other green parts (e.g. green stems)

cards.term: Which leaf cells have many chloroplasts?
cards.definition: Mesophyll cells

cards.term: How do chloroplasts align in mesophyll cells?
cards.definition:
Along the cell walls to get optimum light.
Flat surfaces face the light in low light and turn parallel (edge-on) to it in strong light

cards.term: Division of labour in the chloroplast?
cards.definition: Membranes (grana): trap light, make ATP and NADPH. Stroma: enzymatic reactions make sugar, then starch.

cards.term: Why are "dark reactions" not really dark reactions?
cards.definition: They don't need light directly but depend on ATP and NADPH from the light reaction; they do not occur in darkness. Better name: carbon reactions or biosynthetic phase.

cards.term: Figure 11.2 · Chloroplast (electron micrograph)
Four leaf pigments separated by paper chromatography, with colours?
cards.definition:
Chlorophyll a: bright/blue green
Chlorophyll b: yellow green
Xanthophylls: yellow
Carotenoids: yellow to yellow-orange

cards.text: Chlorophyll a appears {{c1::bright or blue green}}; chlorophyll b appears {{c2::yellow green}} on a chromatogram.

cards.term: What are pigments?
cards.definition: Substances that absorb light at specific wavelengths

cards.term: Most abundant plant pigment in the world?
cards.definition: Chlorophyll a

cards.term: In which colours does chlorophyll a absorb most?
cards.definition: Blue and red

cards.term: Absorption spectrum vs action spectrum?
cards.definition:
Absorption: how much light a pigment absorbs at each wavelength
Action: rate of photosynthesis at each wavelength

cards.term: Why is chlorophyll a called the chief pigment?
cards.definition: Its absorption peaks (blue, red) match the peaks of the action spectrum

cards.term: Do the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a and the action spectrum overlap exactly?
cards.definition: No. Some photosynthesis happens at other wavelengths, thanks to accessory pigments.

cards.term: Name the accessory pigments.
cards.definition: Chlorophyll b, xanthophylls, carotenoids

cards.term: Two roles of accessory pigments?
cards.definition:
Absorb a wider range of wavelengths and pass energy to chlorophyll a
Protect chlorophyll a from photo-oxidation

cards.term: A plant with chlorophyll b but no chlorophyll a: would it photosynthesise?
cards.definition: No. Chlorophyll a forms the reaction centre; accessory pigments only pass energy to it.

cards.term: Why does a leaf kept in the dark turn yellow?
cards.definition: Chlorophyll breaks down and is not remade without light; the more stable carotenoids remain

cards.term: Shade leaves vs sun leaves: which are darker green, and why?
cards.definition: Shade leaves: more chlorophyll to catch the limited light

cards.term: What does the light reaction (photochemical phase) include?
cards.definition: Light absorption, water splitting, oxygen release, and formation of ATP and NADPH

cards.term: Into what are the pigments organised?
cards.definition: Two light harvesting complexes (LHC) within PS I and PS II

cards.term: Why is PS I called "I" even though PS II acts first?
cards.definition: Photosystems are named by the order of discovery, not the order they function

cards.term: What is the antenna?
cards.definition:
All the pigments of a photosystem (hundreds, bound to proteins) except the reaction centre chlorophyll a.
They harvest light

cards.term: What forms the reaction centre?
cards.definition: A single chlorophyll a molecule

cards.text: Reaction centre of PS I = {{c1::P700}}; of PS II = {{c2::P680}}.

cards.term: Mnemonic: which reaction centre is PS II?
cards.definition: "Two eight" is the first to act: PS II = P680 (shorter wavelength, acts first); PS I = P700.

cards.term: Figure 11.4 · Light harvesting complex
What happens when P680 absorbs red light?
cards.definition: Electrons are excited and picked up by an electron acceptor, then passed to an ETS of cytochromes

cards.term: Are electrons used up in the ETS between PS II and PS I?
cards.definition: No. They pass downhill (redox scale) to the pigments of PS I.

cards.term: Where do electrons from PS I finally go?
cards.definition: To NADP⁺, reducing it to NADPH + H⁺

cards.term: What is the Z scheme?
cards.definition:
The electron path PS II → acceptor → ETS → PS I → acceptor → NADP⁺.
It looks like a Z when carriers are placed on a redox potential scale

cards.term: Figure 11.5 · Z scheme of light reaction
How does PS II get its electrons replaced?
cards.definition: By splitting of water

cards.term: Water splitting equation?
cards.definition: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + O₂ + 4e⁻

cards.term: Water splitting is associated with which photosystem?
cards.definition: PS II

cards.term: On which side of the thylakoid membrane is the water-splitting complex?
cards.definition: The inner side (lumen side); so H⁺ and O₂ are released into the lumen

cards.term: Where do the electrons that replace those lost by PS I come from?
cards.definition: From PS II

cards.term: What is photophosphorylation?
cards.definition: Synthesis of ATP from ADP and Pi in the presence of light

cards.term: What is non-cyclic photophosphorylation?
cards.definition: PS II and PS I work in series (Z scheme); makes both ATP and NADPH

cards.term: What is cyclic photophosphorylation?
cards.definition: Only PS I works the electron cycles back to PS I through the ETS only ATP is made, no NADPH

cards.term: Where may cyclic photophosphorylation occur, and why there?
cards.definition: In the stroma lamellae: they lack PS II and NADP reductase

cards.term: When else does cyclic photophosphorylation occur?
cards.definition: When only light of wavelength beyond 680 nm is available

cards.term: Grana lamellae vs stroma lamellae: photosystems?
cards.definition: Grana: PS I and PS II. Stroma lamellae: PS I only.

cards.term: Cyclic vs non-cyclic photophosphorylation
cards.definition: Photosystems: Cyclic: PS I · Non-cyclic: PS I + PS II; Products: Cyclic: ATP only · Non-cyclic: ATP + NADPH; Water split, O₂ released?: Cyclic: no · Non-cyclic: yes; Location: Cyclic: stroma lamellae · Non-cyclic: grana

cards.term: What does the chemiosmotic hypothesis explain?
cards.definition: How ATP is made: ATP synthesis is linked to a proton gradient across a membrane (here the thylakoid)

cards.term: Where do protons accumulate in photosynthesis vs respiration?
cards.definition: Photosynthesis: thylakoid lumen. Respiration: mitochondrial intermembrane space.

cards.term: Three causes of the proton gradient across the thylakoid?
cards.definition: (a) Water splitting inside releases H⁺ into the lumen. (b) The primary acceptor passes electrons to an H carrier, which moves H⁺ from stroma to lumen. (c) NADP reductase on the stroma side uses up H⁺ from the stroma.

cards.term: What happens to lumen pH during the light reaction?
cards.definition: It decreases (more acidic) as H⁺ accumulates

cards.term: How does the gradient make ATP?
cards.definition:
H⁺ flow back to the stroma through the CF₀ channel of ATP synthase.
The energy changes the conformation of CF₁, which makes ATP

cards.text: ATP synthase: {{c1::CF₀}} is embedded in the membrane and forms the proton channel; {{c2::CF₁}} protrudes on the stroma side and makes ATP.

cards.term: Four requirements of chemiosmosis?
cards.definition: A membrane, a proton pump, a proton gradient and ATP synthase

cards.term: Figure 11.7: trace the protons.
cards.definition:
H⁺ from water splitting and the PQ shuttle collect in the lumen (high H⁺).
They return to the stroma (low H⁺) through ATP synthase, making ATP

cards.term: Intuition: chemiosmosis is like a…?
cards.definition:
A dam:
the light reaction pumps water (H⁺) uphill into the reservoir (lumen);
ATP synthase is the turbine it flows back through

cards.term: Products of the light reaction and their fate?
cards.definition: O₂ diffuses out; ATP and NADPH drive sugar synthesis in the stroma

cards.term: How can you show the biosynthetic phase depends on light products?
cards.definition: After light is switched off it continues briefly then stops; it restarts when light returns

cards.term: Which isotope did Calvin use, and in what organism?
cards.definition: ¹⁴C, in algal photosynthesis

cards.term: First stable product of CO₂ fixation found by Calvin?
cards.definition: 3-phosphoglyceric acid (PGA): a 3-carbon acid

cards.term: First product in C4 plants?
cards.definition: Oxaloacetic acid (OAA): a 4-carbon acid

cards.term: Primary CO₂ acceptor in the Calvin cycle?
cards.definition: Ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP): a 5-carbon ketose sugar

cards.term: Why did scientists first look for a 2-carbon CO₂ acceptor?
cards.definition: The first product (PGA) had 3 carbons, so they assumed 2 + 1. It was actually 5 + 1 → 2 × 3.

cards.term: Does the Calvin cycle occur in C4 plants too?
cards.definition: Yes. It occurs in all photosynthetic plants.

cards.term: What is carboxylation?
cards.definition: Fixation of CO₂ into a stable organic intermediate: RuBP + CO₂ → 2 × 3-PGA, by RuBisCO

cards.term: Most crucial step of the Calvin cycle?
cards.definition: Carboxylation

cards.term: Why is RuBP carboxylase better called RuBisCO?
cards.definition: It also has oxygenase activity: RuBP carboxylase-oxygenase

cards.term: Reduction step uses what per CO₂ fixed?
cards.definition: 2 ATP (phosphorylation) and 2 NADPH (reduction)

cards.term: Regeneration step uses what per CO₂?
cards.definition: 1 ATP to regenerate RuBP

cards.term: ATP and NADPH per CO₂ fixed?
cards.definition: 3 ATP and 2 NADPH

cards.term: How many turns of the Calvin cycle make one glucose?
cards.definition: 6 (6 CO₂ fixed)

cards.term: Calvin cycle: inputs and outputs per glucose
cards.definition: 6 CO₂: 1 glucose; 18 ATP: 18 ADP; 12 NADPH: 12 NADP⁺

cards.term: Why is cyclic photophosphorylation needed?
cards.definition:
Calvin cycle needs ATP : NADPH = 3 : 2.
Non-cyclic flow gives them roughly equally, so cyclic flow makes the extra ATP

cards.term: Figure 11.8 · Calvin cycle
Where are C4 plants adapted?
cards.definition: Dry tropical regions

cards.term: Main biosynthetic pathway in C4 plants?
cards.definition: Still the Calvin cycle (C3 pathway)

cards.term: Special features of C4 plants?
cards.definition:
Kranz anatomy
Tolerate higher temperatures
Respond to high light
Lack photorespiration
Greater biomass productivity

cards.term: What is Kranz anatomy?
cards.definition: Large bundle sheath cells around vascular bundles, arranged like a wreath

cards.term: What does "Kranz" mean?
cards.definition: Wreath

cards.term: Features of bundle sheath cells in C4 plants?
cards.definition: Many chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gas exchange, no intercellular spaces; may form several layers

cards.term: Examples of C4 plants?
cards.definition: Maize, sorghum (also sugarcane)

cards.term: Can you tell C3 from C4 by looking at a plant from outside?
cards.definition: Not reliably. You need a leaf section to see Kranz anatomy.

cards.term: Other name of the C4 pathway?
cards.definition: Hatch and Slack pathway

cards.term: Primary CO₂ acceptor in C4 plants?
cards.definition: Phosphoenol pyruvate (PEP): 3-carbon, in mesophyll cells

cards.term: Enzyme that fixes CO₂ in C4 mesophyll?
cards.definition: PEP carboxylase (PEPcase)

cards.term: Do C4 mesophyll cells have RuBisCO?
cards.definition: No

cards.term: C4 pathway steps?
cards.definition:
Mesophyll: PEP + CO₂ → OAA → malic or aspartic acid
Bundle sheath: C4 acid breaks down to CO₂ + 3C molecule
CO₂ enters the Calvin cycle
The 3C molecule returns to mesophyll → PEP

cards.term: Bundle sheath cells of C4 plants: RuBisCO and PEPcase?
cards.definition: Rich in RuBisCO, lack PEPcase

cards.term: Where does the Calvin cycle run in C3 vs C4 plants?
cards.definition: C3: all mesophyll cells. C4: only bundle sheath cells.

cards.term: C4 plants run the Calvin cycle in few cells yet are more productive. Why?
cards.definition: CO₂ is concentrated at RuBisCO in bundle sheath cells, so there is no photorespiration

cards.term: Most abundant enzyme in the world?
cards.definition: RuBisCO

cards.term: Why can RuBisCO bind O₂?
cards.definition: Its active site binds both CO₂ and O₂; binding is competitive and depends on their relative concentrations

cards.term: When does RuBisCO favour CO₂?
cards.definition: When CO₂ : O₂ is nearly equal (it has much greater affinity for CO₂)

cards.term: What happens in photorespiration?
cards.definition: RuBP + O₂ → one phosphoglycerate + one phosphoglycolate (2C)

cards.term: Photorespiration produces sugar, ATP or NADPH?
cards.definition: None. It releases CO₂ and uses ATP.

cards.term: Biological function of photorespiration?
cards.definition: Not known (per NCERT)

cards.term: Beyond NCERT: which organelles take part in photorespiration?
cards.definition:
Chloroplast, peroxisome, mitochondrion
Many scientists now think it protects against photo-damage and recycles carbon lost as glycolate

cards.term: Why don't C4 plants show photorespiration?
cards.definition: C4 acids release CO₂ in bundle sheath cells, raising CO₂ at RuBisCO, so it acts as a carboxylase

cards.term: C3 vs C4: CO₂ fixation rate under high light?
cards.definition: C3: low. C4: high.

cards.term: Photorespiration at low vs high CO₂ (C3 plants)?
cards.definition: Low CO₂: high. High CO₂: negligible.

cards.term: Internal (plant) factors affecting photosynthesis?
cards.definition:
Number, size, age and orientation of leaves
mesophyll cells and chloroplasts
internal CO₂
amount of chlorophyll

cards.term: External factors affecting photosynthesis?
cards.definition: Sunlight, temperature, CO₂ concentration, water

cards.term: State Blackman's law of limiting factors (1905).
cards.definition: If a process is affected by more than one factor, its rate is determined by the factor nearest to its minimal value

cards.term: Example of Blackman's law?
cards.definition: A green leaf with optimal light and CO₂ will not photosynthesise if the temperature is very low

cards.term: Three aspects of light as a factor?
cards.definition: Quality, intensity and duration

cards.term: Light intensity vs CO₂ fixation rate?
cards.definition: Linear at low intensity; levels off at high intensity as other factors limit

cards.term: At what fraction of full sunlight does light saturation occur?
cards.definition: 10%

cards.term: Is light usually limiting in nature?
cards.definition: Rarely, except for plants in shade or dense forests

cards.term: What happens with very high light?
cards.definition: Chlorophyll breaks down and photosynthesis decreases

cards.term: Figure 11.10: where is light limiting, and what are C and D?
cards.definition: Region A (rising line): light limiting. Plateau C: other factors limiting (maximum rate). D: light saturation point.

cards.term: Major limiting factor for photosynthesis?
cards.definition: CO₂

cards.term: CO₂ concentration in the atmosphere?
cards.definition: 0.03–0.04%. Up to 0.05% increases fixation; beyond that it can damage over long periods.

cards.term: Update: atmospheric CO₂ today?
cards.definition: About 0.042% (≈420 ppm) and rising; NCERT's 0.03–0.04% is from older data

cards.term: CO₂ saturation points of C4 vs C3?
cards.definition: C4: about 360 µL/L. C3: only beyond 450 µL/L (so current CO₂ limits C3 plants).

cards.term: At low light, do C3 or C4 plants respond to high CO₂?
cards.definition: Neither

cards.term: Which greenhouse crops are grown in CO₂-enriched air?
cards.definition: Tomatoes, bell pepper (C3 plants: higher yield)

cards.term: Light vs dark reactions: temperature sensitivity?
cards.definition: Dark reactions (enzymatic) are temperature controlled; light reactions are affected much less

cards.term: C3 vs C4 temperature optimum?
cards.definition: C4: higher. C3: much lower. Tropical plants have higher optima than temperate plants.

cards.term: How does water stress reduce photosynthesis?
cards.definition: Stomata close (less CO₂); leaves wilt (less surface area and metabolic activity). The effect is on the plant, not directly on the reaction.

cards.term: Correction: NCERT's summary says electrons go "finally to NAD forming NADH". What is right?
cards.definition: In photosynthesis the final acceptor is NADP⁺, forming NADPH. NAD⁺/NADH is used in respiration.

cards.term: Light reaction vs dark reaction: location and products?
cards.definition: Light: thylakoid membranes makes ATP, NADPH, O₂. Dark (carbon): stroma makes sugars using ATP and NADPH.
